speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to the clinic. I understand you are presenting with a generalized nonpruritic rash, a recent history of high fever, and a seizure. To help me determine the cause, can you tell me exactly when the fever started and how high it reached?

speaker: Patient
text: 9-month-old infant. The patient is brought in due to a generalized nonpruritic rash for 2 days. The rash started on the trunk and spread to the extremities. Five days ago, the patient had a fever of 40.5°C (104.9°F) and experienced a 1-minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure. The infant was born at term, has no history of serious illness, and her immunizations are up to date. The current medication includes acetaminophen.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Roseola Infantum (Exanthem Subitum).

The clinical picture of a 9-month-old with a high fever (>40°C) followed by a seizure and then a generalized, non-pruritic rash that started on the trunk is classic for Roseola Infantum, caused by Human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) or 7 (HHV-7).

Given the history of a seizure, I would like to request an EEG to rule out any lingering epileptic activity, though the fever likely provoked the event. REQUEST TEST: EEG. Additionally, please return the admission photos of the rash for confirmation. REQUEST IMAGES.
